parts.title: Part 1

passage.title: Earthquakes
passage.content:
Scientists say we need a new category for earthquakes. This is because tectonic activity is causing more powerful quakes. The _____ want to extend the current 1 to 10 scale used to measure earthquakes. A category 10 is currently the strongest. This is when magnitudes reach 9.0 on the Richter scale. The scientists say a new category of 11 is needed for magnitudes of over 9.5. They say that in the past decade, there have been several _____ that would be a category 11. Earthquakes can occur anywhere in the world, but are most common along _____ plate boundaries.

A seismologist said the USA's Geological Survey would need to start researching intense quakes to create the _____ 11. He wants more discussions, "about how to better prepare for risk in a tectonically active world". He said human activities, such as mining and reservoir-induced seismicity, are increasing the chances of stronger quakes. This is causing more energy to be released, which makes earthquakes more powerful. The _____ thinks there will be more "mega-quakes" in the future. He said: "These _____ keep getting stronger as tectonic activities increase."

questions.hint: The _____ want to extend the current scale
The _____ thinks there will be more mega-quakes

parts.instruction: Read the text. Fill in each gap with ONE word. You must use a word which is somewhere in the rest of the text.

q1.text: The first sentence introduces the 'scientists' who believe a new category is needed. The sentence with the gap refers to this same group of people who want to change the scale. That's why the correct answer is 'scientists'.
q1.quote: Scientists say we need a new category for earthquakes.

q2.text: The passage discusses creating a new category for very powerful earthquakes. The sentence with the gap refers to recent seismic events that would have fit into this new, higher category. That's why the correct answer is 'earthquakes'.
q2.quote: The scientists say a new category of 11 is needed for magnitudes of over 9.5.

q3.text: The passage states that 'tectonic activity' is causing stronger quakes. The sentence with the gap uses the same adjective to describe the specific type of plate boundaries where earthquakes are common. That's why the correct answer is 'tectonic'.
q3.quote: This is because tectonic activity is causing more powerful quakes.

q4.text: The text repeatedly mentions the need for a 'new category' for earthquakes, specifically a 'category of 11'. The sentence with the gap refers to the action of creating this new classification. That's why the correct answer is 'category'.
q4.quote: The scientists say a new category of 11 is needed for magnitudes of over 9.5.

q5.text: The passage introduces a 'seismologist' who discusses the need for more research. The sentence with the gap continues to describe this same expert's opinion about future seismic events. That's why the correct answer is 'seismologist'.
q5.quote: A seismologist said the USA's Geological Survey would need to start researching intense quakes to create the _____ 11.

q6.text: The seismologist predicts more 'mega-quakes' in the future. The final sentence is a direct quote from him, continuing this thought by using 'quakes', a shortened form of 'earthquakes'. That's why the correct answer is 'quakes'.
q6.quote: This is causing more energy to be released, which makes earthquakes more powerful.

parts.title: Part 4

passage.title: Raisins
passage.content:
Few foods can claim a history as long as the humble raisin. Long before refrigeration or canning existed, people discovered that grapes left in the sun would shrink, darken and keep for months. Archaeological evidence suggests that ancient civilisations in the Middle East were sun-drying grapes as early as 2000 BC, and the practice soon spread across the Mediterranean. The Phoenicians and Armenians carried them along their trade routes, the Romans offered them as prizes in sporting contests, and medieval European physicians prescribed them for everything from coughs to poor digestion. Today raisins are produced and eaten on every inhabited continent, which makes them one of the oldest preserved foods still in daily use.

For the modern food industry, the raisin's greatest asset is its durability. Because most of the water has been removed, raisins resist the growth of bacteria and mould and, if stored correctly, remain edible for up to a year without refrigeration. This long shelf life lowers storage and transport costs, allowing manufacturers to ship them across the globe with little waste. Their versatility is equally valuable: raisins appear in breakfast cereals, cakes, bread, biscuits, sauces and even savoury rice dishes such as Uzbek plov. As a natural sweetener, they also allow producers to reduce the amount of refined sugar added to their products.

Production is dominated by a handful of countries, with Turkey, the United States, Iran and Uzbekistan among the largest suppliers. In California, which grows almost all American raisins, grapes are still largely dried in the open air on paper trays laid between the vines. While this traditional technique has hardly changed, the way the grapes are grown certainly has. The majority of large companies rely on conventional farming, using chemical fertilisers and pesticides to maximise yields. Organic methods, though increasingly popular with consumers, are practised by only a small minority of growers, largely because they require more labour and produce smaller harvests.

This intensive approach comes at a cost. Growing grapes year after year on the same land gradually strips the soil of essential nutrients, leaving it less fertile and ever more dependent on artificial inputs. Moreover, vineyards in dry regions consume enormous quantities of water, and chemicals washed from the fields can enter rivers and streams, harming fish, insects and the birds that feed on them. Environmental groups argue that unless farming practices change, some major growing areas may eventually become unable to support the crop at all.

The human side of the industry raises questions too. The harvest takes place in late summer, when temperatures in California's San Joaquin Valley regularly exceed 40°C. Pickers, many of them seasonal migrants, cut the bunches by hand and are often paid according to the number of trays they fill rather than by the hour. As a result, their earnings frequently fall below those of farm workers in many other American states, despite the exhausting nature of the job.

Nutritionally, raisins have much to recommend them. They are rich in fibre, potassium, iron and antioxidants, and parents often pack them in school lunches as a healthier alternative to sweets. Yet nutritionists urge caution. The drying process concentrates the fruit's natural sugar, so a small handful contains roughly as many calories as a large bowl of fresh grapes. Because raisins are so easy to eat in large quantities, regular overconsumption can contribute to weight gain, type 2 diabetes and tooth decay. In addition, some lighter varieties, known as golden raisins, are treated with sulphur dioxide to preserve their colour, and consumers are advised to read labels carefully.

Looking ahead, scientists are searching for ways to make raisin production more sustainable. Researchers at agricultural universities are developing grape varieties that dry naturally on the vine and require less water, while some farms have begun experimenting with drip irrigation and solar-powered dryers. Others are testing cover crops planted between the rows to restore nutrients to the soil. If these efforts succeed, this ancient food may continue to be enjoyed for centuries to come, with far less damage to the environment.

parts.title: Part 5

passage.title: Electric vehicles
passage.content:
Over the past decade, electric vehicles (EVs) have shifted from being a niche curiosity to a significant presence on the world's roads. According to the International Energy Agency, electric cars made up around fourteen percent of all new cars sold globally in 2022, a remarkable rise from just four percent only two years earlier. Industry analysts predict that this figure will continue to climb as manufacturers expand their electric line-ups and consumers become increasingly aware of environmental issues.

Surprisingly, the electric car is not a modern invention. As early as the late nineteenth century, electric models competed directly with steam and petrolpowered vehicles. In fact, around 1900, they were particularly popular among wealthy urban residents, who appreciated their quiet operation and the convenience of not having to start the engine with a heavy hand crank. However, the mass production of cheap petrol cars, combined with the discovery of vast oil reserves, gradually pushed electric vehicles off the market for most of the twentieth century.

The recent revival of electric transport can be attributed to several factors. Advances in lithium-ion battery technology have significantly reduced costs while increasing the distance a vehicle can travel on a single charge. At the same time, governments across the globe have introduced subsidies, tax exemptions and stricter emission standards, all of which have stimulated consumer demand. Many countries have even announced plans to ban the sale of new petrol and diesel cars within the next two decades.

Despite this progress, many motorists remain hesitant to make the switch. One of the most frequently cited concerns is so-called range anxiety, the fear that a vehicle's battery will run out before the driver reaches a charging point. Although modern EVs can typically cover between 300 and 500 kilometres on a full battery, this worry continues to influence purchasing decisions, particularly among people who live in rural areas or regularly undertake long journeys.

Range is not the only obstacle. In many regions, the public charging network remains underdeveloped, leaving drivers with few options outside major cities. Recharging a battery also takes considerably longer than filling a tank with fuel, sometimes requiring several hours. Furthermore, the initial purchase price of an electric car is still higher than that of a comparable conventional model, and batteries gradually lose their capacity over time, which can reduce the vehicle's resale value.

The environmental benefits of electric cars are also the subject of ongoing debate. While EVs produce no exhaust emissions, critics point out that their overall impact depends largely on how the electricity used to charge them is generated. In countries that rely heavily on coal-fired power stations, the reduction in carbon emissions may be relatively modest. In addition, the extraction of raw materials such as lithium and cobalt, which are essential for battery production, raises serious environmental and ethical concerns.

Nevertheless, most experts agree that electric vehicles will play a central role in the future of transport. As renewable energy sources expand, charging infrastructure improves and battery technology continues to advance, many of today's limitations are likely to be overcome. The transition may not be immediate, but the direction of change appears increasingly clear.
